disease_info: Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features is characterized by at least one fully syndromal manic episode, often with marked impairment in functioning, that may be accompanied by delusions or hallucinations congruent or incongruent with mood. Episodes typically develop over days to weeks, can last weeks to months if untreated, and may alternate with depressive episodes or periods of relative euthymia. Psychotic features usually emerge at the more severe end of mania, often involving grandiose or paranoid themes, and help distinguish it from hypomania in Bipolar II Disorder. Clinically, it must be differentiated from primary psychotic disorders and substance- or medication-induced conditions by the temporal relationship of mood and psychosis, the episodic course, family history, and response to mood stabilizers.

narrative.personality: Cristian is a detail-obsessed, quietly anxious craftsman who blends perfectionistic workmanship with a sentimental, artistic streak and a tendency to overprepare for everything.
narrative.stressor: In the year leading up to onset, Cristian had built a reputation in his city for highly customized smart-home water systems and decorative metal work, and he took on an unusually large commercial contract that required him to act as both lead contractor and designer. The project ran into permitting delays, cost overruns, and conflicts with the general contractor, all while he was trying to keep his small business afloat and support extended family members who had moved into his home, leaving him sleeping less and worrying constantly about his reputation and finances. As pressure mounted, he began throwing himself into ever more ambitious side projects tied to the contract, insisting on personally overseeing every detail, staying up most nights sketching elaborate designs, and making increasingly risky business decisions that alarmed his wife and long-time clients. Over roughly three months, his behavior became so uncharacteristically expansive, erratic, and tied to unrealistic beliefs about what he could achieve that he jeopardized the contract and family savings, leading to a crisis meeting with his wife and brother who insisted he see a psychiatrist after he signed several large, uncompensated bids and nearly lost a major client.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I keep getting carried away with these big projects and business moves that end up costing us and putting my family at risk.”

narrative.personality: Anabelle is an energetic, sociable apprentice who loves being busy, thrives on learning hands-on skills, and tends to dive impulsively into new experiences and social scenes.
narrative.stressor: Anabelle had just graduated high school and moved from her mother’s home into a shared apartment closer to the community college and the HVAC company where she’d started her apprenticeship, a transition she embraced as proof that she could be fully independent. Between juggling early-morning service calls, evening classes, and a lively new social circle that revolved around late-night dancing and weekend festivals, she began sleeping less and packing her days with back-to-back commitments, proud of how much she could fit into a week. Over several weeks, her drive to take on more grew beyond what her supervisors and friends saw as typical for her, as she volunteered for extra shifts, organized multiple community projects, and launched several personal side ideas all at once, becoming increasingly scattered and hard to redirect. When she started missing safety steps on jobs, arguing with her lead tech about unrealistic plans, and showing up exhausted but still insisting she could “do everything,” her supervisor and an aunt grew concerned and encouraged her to seek psychiatric evaluation after a near-miss electrical incident on a call.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I feel like I can’t slow down—I’m constantly on the go and taking on more and more.”

narrative.personality: Zachary is a highly analytical, competitive professional who channels his intensity into data-driven problem solving, outdoor challenges, and a tendency to overthink every decision.
narrative.stressor: In the months before onset, Zachary was promoted to a higher-stakes role at his bank just as the firm began restructuring its risk models in response to economic uncertainty, increasing scrutiny on his analyses and recommendations. Determined to prove himself, he started working very long hours, simultaneously maintaining his demanding fitness and outdoor routines and taking on a self-initiated machine-learning side project to outdo competing teams, leaving little room for rest or recovery. Gradually, his usual methodical style gave way to an increasingly scattered focus as he chased every new idea, toggling between work spreadsheets, personal trading schemes, and side coding projects, while becoming preoccupied with patterns he believed he alone could see in markets and daily events. After several months in which his productivity became erratic, he clashed with colleagues over grandiose proposals, missed critical deadlines, and made impulsive financial decisions that affected both his own investments and team outputs; his manager and a close friend intervened when he appeared unable to filter irrelevant from important information and strongly urged a psychiatric evaluation.
narrative.chief_complaint: “My mind keeps jumping to every little thing around me and I can’t stay focused on what I’m supposed to be doing.”
